To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) energy prices and market size affect the innovation decisions of small specialized firms more than those of large mixed firms, and (ii) the effect of energy prices and market sizes is larger at the extensive margin (i.e. entry and exit) than at the intensive margin.

(1) firms' innovation decisions are driven by energy prices, market potential and knowledge stocks; (2) the entry and exit decisions of firms are more important to redirect innovation towards renewable than to large firms' innovation decisions; and (3) the entry decisions of firms are driven by energy price changes, market potential and R&D stock.

1) the entry of small specialized firms is a crucial factor for redirecting innovation towards renewable energy technologies; 2) energy prices and market sizes matter to redirect innovation; 3) knowledge stocks matter to redirect innovation, but less than energy prices and market size; and 4) the impact of knowledge stocks is larger on closing the technology gaps between renewable and fossil-fuel technologies through entry and exit of specialized firms, rather through innovation of large mixed firms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the determinants of the shift of technical change from fossil fuel to renewable energy innovation.
the determinants of the extensive margin (i.e. the entry/exit of small specialized firms) of directed technical change, which has been largely ignored in the empirical literature so far.
how firms' decisions to conduct R&D and the direction of that R&D are affected by energy prices, market conditions and knowledge stocks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the entry (exit) of small specialized REN firms, which innovate only in renewable technologies, is the most important determinant of directed technical change in the electricity generation industry.

our results suggest that the entry of new firms, the exit of old firms, and the innovation of incumbent firms are all important to redirect the electricity generation industry towards renewable energy technologies.

our results suggest that a combination of policy measures that simultaneously affect energy prices and market size, as well as policies that affect the knowledge stock, may be effective in inducing directed technical change in the electricity generation industry.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
firm dynamics and the interaction with the market and the knowledge stock are key to understanding the diffusion of new technologies.
firm-level dynamics are of policy interest to induce a transition from FF to RENE technologies.

energy prices and knowledge stocks are the key determinants of directed REN innovation, but the market size of REN technologies matters more for entry and exit decisions of specialized REN and FF firms than for innovation by mixed REN and FF large firms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the policy focus should be on the extensive margin innovation of small specialized firms.
the replacement of FF technologies by REN technologies can be induced by policies which increase energy prices, the market size for REN technologies and the knowledge stocks of REN technologies.
policies that increase the market size for REN technologies, or decrease the market size of FF technologies, will have a positive effect on the replacement of FF technologies by REN technologies.
